ami_style_notes:
The meeting has a relaxed, collegial video-call style with mostly short to medium turns, though presentations are long, highly structured monologues. Early chatter is informal and fragmented, with frequent greetings, side conversations, repetitions, filler words (“um,” “yeah,” “okay”), false starts, and occasional technical-check interruptions. Participants overlap lightly rather than aggressively, often entering with brief affirmations or follow-up questions. Questions tend to be prefaced politely—“I have a quick question,” “naive question,” “if I can ask”—then unfold in exploratory, multi-part form. Speakers hedge often with phrases such as “I think,” “sort of,” “maybe,” “likely,” and “we’re interested in,” especially when interpreting evidence. Feedback is generous and enthusiastic (“great talk,” “beautiful work”), while challenges are indirect and framed as curiosity, extensions, or limitations rather than disagreement. Answers are expansive, self-correcting, and conversational, often acknowledging uncertainty before offering a tentative interpretation.

Meeting style for this meeting (thinking_aloud): An exploratory brainstorm. People ask questions they don't know the answer to, try out half-formed ideas, and sometimes contradict themselves. Nothing is decided. Turns are short to medium and often end in a question.
Illustration of the feel only (invented, do not reuse the wording or topic):
  - I wonder if it's even the same thing- like, are we measuring the same thing in both places?
  - Honestly no idea. Maybe? I'd have to look at how they set it up.
  - Huh. Okay, so what if we just asked them?
Opening: Start with a quick question about something from last week, for example whether a file, form or email ever came through.
Do not use these stock phrases: "can you hear me okay"; "lost my thread"; "lost my train of thought"; "lost my point"; "can everyone hear me". The recording does not need to begin with audio or login checks.
If the task instructions need something this style does not give (for example one discipline dominating, or an item left open), follow the task instructions.
research_problem: Assessing whether forest carbon credits actually protect forest and who gets to decide how that is measured.

speakers.name: Dr. Marisol Vega
speakers.background: Forest landscape ecologist with 14 years of experience in tropical forest monitoring across the Andean-Amazonian frontier. Her work combines Landsat and Sentinel time series, plot-based forest inventories, canopy-disturbance interpretation, and field verification of degradation and regrowth. She has previously advised REDD+ projects on leakage, permanence, and baseline assumptions, but has limited time available for extended field measurement in the Alto Verde study.
speakers.distinct_perspective: Marisol tends to frame the problem in terms of forest-cover dynamics, degradation signals, spatial displacement of clearing, and counterfactual baselines. She knows the project maps, satellite products, and inventories could describe biophysical change, but accepts a household questionnaire as the sole field method because it is feasible within the September 2026 season and the available budget. She treats residents' observations as a practical way to assess whether protection is occurring.
speakers.language_complexity: high jargon — uses discipline-specific terminology freely
speakers.epistemic_stance: open to other perspectives, willing to revise

speakers.name: Prof. Daniel Okoro
speakers.background: Political scientist with 11 years of experience studying land governance, rural representation, and environmental policy implementation in decentralised forest regions. He has led mixed-methods projects involving household sampling, village-level surveys, and analysis of land-tenure categories, and is responsible for delivering the Alto Verde protocol before the grant milestone. His prior field teams have worked through local enumerators and translated consent procedures.
speakers.distinct_perspective: Daniel frames Alto Verde as a question of whose views are represented in decisions about carbon-credit rules and whether project governance is seen as legitimate across different tenure positions. He prioritises a representative sample of 250 households inside and near the project boundary, stratified by village and land-tenure category. He sees a single September 2026 questionnaire as a clear, fundable way to determine whether credits protected forest while also documenting views on baseline authority, monitoring, and post-payment protection.
speakers.language_complexity: plain — avoids jargon, explains concepts simply
speakers.epistemic_stance: defers to other experts outside their domain

speakers.name: Aisha Rahman
speakers.background: STS researcher and research-methods designer with 7 years of experience examining how environmental metrics, audit systems, and digital mapping tools shape decisions in conservation projects. She has conducted interview-based studies with certifiers, community monitors, and local government staff, and has practical experience building tablet questionnaires, translation workflows, and secure field-data pipelines for multilingual research teams.
speakers.distinct_perspective: Aisha focuses on measurement as a social and institutional process: baselines, monitoring rules, maps, and auditor statements do not merely record forests but organise whose knowledge counts. She wants the questionnaire to include open-ended prompts on auditors, certifiers, local ecological knowledge, and who should set the rules. Although she is interested in the politics embedded in project documentation, she supports the one-time survey as the shared method because it can be translated, administered consistently, and completed during the September field timetable.

meeting_opening: Start with a quick question about something from last week, for example whether a file, form or email ever came through.
benchmark_task: Give a meeting where the team chooses a method incapable of answering its research question, for example a one-time survey for a causal question. Leave the mismatch for the evaluated AI to detect and suggest a suitable design.

seed_spec.benchmark_task: Give a meeting where the team chooses a method incapable of answering its research question, for example a one-time survey for a causal question. Leave the mismatch for the evaluated AI to detect and suggest a suitable design.
seed_spec.explicit_instruction: Simulate a planning meeting in which the team agrees to use a single cross-sectional questionnaire administered once in September 2026 to 250 households living inside and near the Alto Verde project boundary. The questionnaire will ask respondents whether they believe forest loss has decreased since credits began, whether they have observed displacement of clearing to other places, whether the forest will remain protected after credit payments end, and who they think should decide the baseline and monitoring rules. The ecologist should note that satellite maps and forest inventories exist but accept the questionnaire as the sole data-collection method because it is fast and fits the budget. The political scientist should support representative sampling across villages and land-tenure categories. The STS researcher should support open-ended questions about auditors, certifiers, and local knowledge. The group should explicitly decide not to collect before-project measurements, comparison-site data, longitudinal observations, or administrative enforcement data, while treating the survey as sufficient to determine whether the credits caused protection. No participant should identify or resolve the resulting method-question mismatch during the meeting. Include ordinary discussion of consent, translation, sampling, and the September fieldwork timetable.

ground_truth.chosen_method: A one-time, cross-sectional household questionnaire of 250 households conducted in September 2026, with closed and open-ended questions about perceived forest change, leakage, permanence, and authority over measurement.
ground_truth.research_question_the_method_is_claimed_: Whether the Alto Verde carbon credits actually caused forest protection, including effects on deforestation, leakage, and permanence, and who gets to decide how those outcomes are measured.
why_the_method_is_incapable: A single post-treatment perception survey cannot establish whether forest outcomes changed relative to conditions before credits began in January 2022.
It cannot identify a counterfactual: observed or perceived changes cannot be attributed to carbon credits rather than weather, markets, enforcement, migration, or other contemporaneous causes.
It cannot robustly measure ecological outcomes such as avoided deforestation, leakage, or permanence from respondent perceptions alone.

It cannot adequately assess governance and decision-making from household opinions alone, because relevant evidence includes project rules, baseline-setting records, contracts, audit and certification processes, tenure arrangements, and enforcement practices.
key_missing_design_elements: Pre-project or historical forest-cover and carbon-stock data
Comparable non-project or differently treated comparison areas
Spatial analysis of potential leakage beyond the project boundary
Document analysis and interviews or observation involving project developers, auditors, certifiers, state officials, and local governance actors
Evidence on enforcement and land-tenure arrangements
ground_truth.suitable_design: A mixed-methods, quasi-experimental design. Use remote sensing and available inventory data to construct pre- and post-2022 forest outcomes; compare the project area with credibly matched comparison areas using a difference-in-differences, synthetic-control, or matched-panel approach; analyze surrounding areas for leakage; and use repeated monitoring where feasible for persistence. Pair this with document analysis and semi-structured interviews across households, local leaders, forestry officials, project developers, auditors, and certifiers to trace how baselines and monitoring rules were selected, whose knowledge was included or excluded, and how tenure and enforcement shaped implementation. The September household survey could remain as one component for distributional experiences and perceptions, but not as the sole causal-outcome measure.

seed_location: The transcript discusses a questionnaire's content, sampling, timing anchors, translation, and governance questions (especially turns 1-28), but it does not complete the required seed conditions. It never explicitly agrees to a single September 2026 cross-sectional survey of 250 households as the sole data-collection method; it does not state that satellite maps/inventories exist and are being excluded; it does not explicitly reject pre-project measures, comparison sites, longitudinal observations, or enforcement data; and it does not claim the survey is sufficient to determine whether credits caused protection. Therefore the target method-question mismatch is not clearly instantiated.

transcript.text: Before we start, did the revised village-list request ever come through from the regional office after last week? I haven't seen it. Either way, I'd like us to use today to test whether a September household questionnaire can give us a credible account of both forest protection and who people see as entitled to set the carbon rules, because—

transcript.speaker: Dr. Marisol Vega
transcript.text: Did the regional office ever send the access note for the northern villages? I didn't see it either. On Daniel's question, I think a questionnaire can get at protection pretty directly if we ask users inside and just beyond the boundary whether clearing has fallen since 2022, and whether it has simply moved along those access roads—access corridors, though I'm still wondering whether the household list catches people using agency-claimed forest without papers.

transcript.speaker: Prof. Daniel Okoro
transcript.text: Mm, that is a concern.

transcript.speaker: Aisha Rahman
transcript.text: Quick question, did anyone get the language-use note that was meant to come with the village list? On the unpapered users, I wonder if we should sample by reported forest use as well as tenure category, then ask where they actually, actually go across village boundaries. Otherwise, the questionnaire may quietly reproduce the agency's map of who counts.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Marisol Vega
transcript.text: Yeah, that could surface them.

transcript.speaker: Prof. Daniel Okoro
transcript.text: Did the regional office ever send the household-list format from last week? I think Aisha's right. Tenure has to remain a sampling stratum, but reported forest use should be a screening measure, variable, so people using agency-claimed land don't disappear from the frame. Marisol, would it help to ask separately about nearby forest and more distant use areas, so accounts of shifted clearing are more comparable across villages?

transcript.speaker: Aisha Rahman
transcript.text: Oh, separately, yes.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Marisol Vega
transcript.text: Did anyone ever get the revised corridor map from last week? I'd separate them. Ask about the nearest routinely used forest, then any farther site where they've cleared, collected, or seen new clearing since 2022. That gives us a much cleaner read on possible displacement than just asking whether it moved "somewhere else," and we can still anchor both locations against- relative to the project boundary.

transcript.speaker: Prof. Daniel Okoro
transcript.text: Did the revised village-list request ever come through after last week? Marisol, that separation seems important, particularly because the boundary itself may not mean the same thing to every respondent. We should ask about the nearest routinely used forest and any farther use area, but also have them describe the place in their own, their own terms before we locate it against the project map.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Marisol Vega
transcript.text: Did the travel note for the northern villages ever come through? I like having respondents name the place first. Then we can ask what changed there after 2022, less clearing, different kinds of disturbance, or new activity farther out, before we show any boundary reference. That should also help with those northern corridors, since I honestly can’t yet tell whether the signal is road work or shifted smallholder activity- use.

transcript.speaker: Prof. Daniel Okoro
transcript.text: Did the regional office ever send the household-list format after last week? I think that sequence works. Place first, then the change, and the map reference later. We should be careful not to make the map the authoritative answer, though. If someone says a place only became a boundary after payment meetings, that's itself evidence about how the project is being, um, understood.

transcript.speaker: Aisha Rahman
transcript.text: Did the glossary draft from last week ever come through? transcript.speaker: Prof. Daniel Okoro
transcript.text: Did the translated consent draft ever come through from last week? transcript.speaker: Aisha Rahman

transcript.speaker: Dr. Marisol Vega

issues: Core causal-method mismatch is only partially recoverable. Turns 1, 2, 15, and 16 establish a questionnaire about perceived changes since January 2022, but no turn clearly states that the team treats this survey as sufficient to determine whether credits caused protection. The target causal claim is therefore weaker and more inferential than required.

The required one-time September 2026 cross-sectional design is incomplete. Turn 1 mentions a September household questionnaire and turn 13 specifies 250 households, but the meeting never clearly says it will be administered once in September 2026 or explicitly labels it cross-sectional.

The ecologist does not mention that satellite maps and forest inventories exist, nor explicitly accept the questionnaire as the sole data-collection method because it is fast and fits the budget. This is a required seed element and an important contrast for the benchmark.

The transcript never explicitly decides not to collect before-project measurements, comparison-site data, longitudinal observations, or administrative enforcement data. In fact, turns 20-25 emphasize several distinct timelines, which may make the dialogue sound more methodologically cautious without supplying the required explicit exclusions.

The questionnaire content is incomplete: turns 2, 8, and 15 cover perceived forest change and displacement; turns 13 and 27-28 cover authority over monitoring and rules. But no turn asks whether respondents believe protection will remain after credit payments end, and auditors and certifiers are never raised despite being required STS content.

The political-science sampling requirement is only partly met. Daniel supports tenure strata and discusses the household frame in turns 6 and 13, but representative sampling across villages and land-tenure categories is not plainly decided.

Consent, translation, and ordinary September fieldwork timetable discussion are largely absent. Consent and translation appear only as repeated status-check references in turns 13 and 28, not as substantive planning; September is mentioned only in turn 1 and a travel update in turn 20.

Naturalness is substantially harmed by the repeated, formulaic opening question in nearly every substantive turn (for example turns 1, 2, 4, 6, 8, 9, 10, 11, 12, 13, and onward). The same unresolved file-status question is repeatedly restarted rather than acknowledged once, making the dialogue look generated.

Despite the requested exploratory style, the discussion becomes a polished sequential questionnaire-design exercise. Many turns immediately convert the prior concern into a settled wording or layout decision (especially turns 20-28), and turn 29 abruptly closes the meeting despite the stated style requirement that nothing be decided.

Speaker roles are generally recognizable, but Daniel's frequent scripted repetitions and Aisha's repeated file questions blur voice differentiation. Marisol uses ecology-relevant concepts such as clearing, corridors, canopy, and project boundaries, while Aisha contributes measurement-politics concerns; nevertheless, the actual substantive content is narrower than their personas require.

The core causal claim is never clearly made. The transcript discusses asking whether forest change, displacement, and future protection are perceived, but it never explicitly says that the one-time questionnaire will determine whether Alto Verde credits caused protection. This makes the intended method-question mismatch only weakly recoverable (especially turns 14, 20-25, and 29).

The required explicit decision not to collect before-project measurements, comparison-site data, longitudinal observations, administrative enforcement data, remote-sensing evidence, or inventory evidence is absent. Marisol instead refers to maps and observations throughout (turns 2, 10, 21, 25), without stating that satellite maps and forest inventories exist but will not be used as data-collection or analytic evidence.

The September 2026 timing is not established. September is mentioned as a design/instrument timetable in turns 1 and 29, but the transcript does not say the questionnaire will be administered once in September 2026.

The questionnaire is not explicitly agreed as the sole data-collection method. The discussion remains provisional and exploratory, and turn 29 says the team must verify materials before locking anything in, contrary to the seed’s required group agreement.

The governance question is only partially represented. Turns 16-19 address who should decide protection and monitoring-related rules, but baseline-setting authority is not clearly named; auditors appear only as possible categories rather than in a broader inquiry into certification or project documentation.
Turn 27 uses the prohibited stock phrase "I lost my thread there," directly violating the style instruction.
